posts.c: "Vancouver’s most VIBRANT neighborhood is historic Chinatown," says CNT Local Creator @ben.glassco. "It's the largest in Canada and stands as a living, breathing heartbeat of the city…and Canada itself. The Gold Rush of the 1850s first brought Chinese migrants to the West Coast, and soon thousands of laborers infamously gave their lives on the Canadian Pacific Railway. Few communities accepted Chinese migrants, so they were forced to build their own. Chinatown rose above systemic persecution to become the center of trade, nightlife, and culture in the new 'Western Canada.' Today, steaming woks, trendy pop-ups, and vibrant speakeasies still fill the gritty but exciting streets—a testament to 150 years of tenacity from the founding peoples of our country." — CNT Local Creator @ben.glassco @ben.glassco's Top Recommendations: Newtown Bakery (slide 7) @chinatownbbq @thechineseteashop by Daniel Lui (slide 12) @chinatownstorytellingcentre (slide 15) @whereisbagheera (slide 4) @baldyloxvintage

posts.c: Rubbing at his eyes carefully with one hand and murmuring “shit” under his breath as he watched one of his slippers tumble toward the ground over 500 meters below, actor Tom Cruise reportedly woke up Wednesday while sleep-climbing the Burj Khalifa. “Oh, no, not this again,” said Cruise, who tightened his grip on the exterior of the skyscraper and then used his feet to bang on the window as hard as he could in a futile bid to attract the attention of a vacuuming custodian. “Hey! Hello! Can you hear me? Let me in! Oh, well. This certainly explains the dream I was having about being a tiny little ant scaling the leg of a picnic table. At least I have pajamas on this time.” At press time, Cruise was scanning the horizon for landing airplanes in the hopes he could jump onto a wing and hitch a ride back to the ground.

posts.c: 🎾 Seasonal tennis courts shut down — starting the week of November 9, @btvparks will begin removing tennis and pickleball nets from courts throughout Burlington and turning off the overhead lights at the Leddy Park courts. At all court facilities, except for Schmanska Park, one court will remain available through the end of November. Removing the nets helps protect court surfaces and infrastructure during the winter months. Freeze-thaw cycles, combined with the tension on the nets, place additional stress on pavement and net anchors, increasing the risk of cracks and damage to both pavement and concrete. Thanks for your partnership!

posts.c: Outside the grand marble church in downtown Middlebury, the night was dark and crisp. Stars sparkled overhead. A warm glow radiated through the stained glass windows. Congregants from across Addison County arrived in small groups, swinging open the heavy doors of St. Mary’s Catholic church, which were decorated with wreaths of orange and yellow paper marigolds and painted sugar skulls. They had assembled for a special Sunday evening Spanish-language Mass in honor of Día de los Muertos, or Day of the Dead, a Mexican holiday with Catholic and Indigenous roots that is held on November 1 and 2. Families gather to joyfully remember deceased loved ones, welcoming their spirits for a brief visit. Vibrant altars offer them drinks, flowers, candles and a sweet bread called pan de muerto. After Mass, the congregants would join a lively procession through the Middlebury College campus, where students performed traditional dances and theatrical renditions of Mexican folk tales. posts.c: In 2015, then-governor Peter Shumlin stood a few feet from Lake Champlain by the Burlington waterfront and signed Vermont’s Clean Water Act. It promised to tighten limits on pollution and provide funding to clean up the state’s waterways. The move was a response to ratcheting pressure from environmentalists and the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency. The EPA had been telling Vermont officials for years that they needed to take much stronger action. In 2016, the agency finalized tougher cleanup targets that the state must meet by 2036. But after 10 years and nearly a billion dollars spent on water quality projects and programs, the Lake Champlain cleanup effort is faltering. In a little-noticed letter to the head of Vermont’s Department of Environmental Conservation last year, the EPA’s regional administrator warned that the state was “not on track” to meet its cleanup goal and would need to more than double its annual pace. posts.c: @royalgorgerouterr is a 150-year-old route winding along the Arkansas River, a geological wonder nicknamed the “Grand Canyon of the Arkansas River.” Visitors can experience the dramatic 10-mile-long chasm from several perspectives: From above, while gazing down from the Royal Gorge Bridge, the tallest suspension bridge in the nation (or for more adventurous travelers, while rock climbing a 5-hour via ferrata); and from below, while paddling the Arkansas’s roaring rapids on a whitewater raft. But for travelers looking to sit back and savor the scenery passing by, there's no better viewpoint than the Royal Gorge Route Railroad's open-air car, standing face-to-face with the staggering canyon walls. Read @kutasarah's full story of her front-row seat to one of Colorado’s greatest natural wonders at the link in bio.

posts.c: On National Bison Day, we celebrate one of America’s most iconic animals and a powerful symbol of strength and resilience. Once reduced to fewer than 1,000 individuals, bison have made a remarkable comeback thanks to decades of dedicated conservation efforts. Today, the National Park Service supports 19 bison herds across 12 states, helping ensure these magnificent animals continue to roam the landscape. Of course, majestic doesn’t mean approachable. Bison are wild, unpredictable, and considerably less interested in meeting you than you might be in meeting them. No matter how calm or cow-like they appear, always stay at least 25 yards away. Finally, if you encounter bison on the road, remember: they’re in no hurry, and your schedule is not their concern. Slow down, stay in your vehicle, and patiently wait for them to move along. Honking or driving aggressively toward bison won’t make them move faster. In fact, it may have the opposite effect. NPS photos

posts.c: One of the things I find most extraordinary about polar bears is the immense journeys they undertake over a lifetime. Guided by a sense of smell seven times more powerful than a blood hound’s, they can detect a seal hidden beneath layers of snow and ice from more than half a mile away. They spend much of their lives following invisible trails of scent across hundreds of miles of Arctic wilderness. This is also how they find one another across a vast, seemingly desolate landscape, although finding mates has become more of a challenge as sea ice recedes. They are the great nomads of the Arctic, always inquisitive, resourceful, and, above all, fiercely determined to navigate a formidable and ever-changing world. For those interested in owning one of my polar bear prints, please visit the link in my bio or visit my website to submit an inquiry. posts.c: Climb ev’ry mountain, Gnaw ev’ry tree, The summit is calling, Living the porcupine dream. Porcupines are creatures of habit. They can spend days hanging out in the same tree, nibbling on bark and needles and quite content with their accommodations. But this particular porcupine has other plans. Not content to keep its paws at lower elevations, it’s steadily making its way uphill, navigating rocks and small plants with the determination of someone who has decided the grass really is greener higher up. Perhaps there’s a better tree waiting at the top. Perhaps it’s simply looking for a change of scenery. What we do know is that this porcupine is going places….mostly uphill. Perhaps to find its dream. NPS video/R. Buchanan: A porcupine walks uphill amid rocks and small plants @mountrainiernps Music of Climb every mountain plays.

posts.c: Ocean in Motion / La Danza del Mar invites the young and young at heart to connect with ocean life through movement and play. The ocean moves us! Hold on like a seahorse—there are plenty of them here and so much more to discover! Just swipe left and sea. African penguins are back in a newly expanded habitat! Watch as they groom and dive off the rocks. Then, practice your penguin waddle in this new interactive space. A 20-foot-long coral reef includes giant clams and a bluespotted ribbontail ray that glides along the sand. Nearby, clownfish nestle into anemones. Enjoy multiple play areas that are welcoming to visitors of all ages. There’s also plenty of rest areas to relax and check out the ocean views of Monterey Bay! Watch leaping blennies hop across wet stones! Visitors can also follow shapes in the floor to hop from rock to rock like blennies. There’s so much to discover in Ocean in Motion / La Danza del Mar from flamboyant cuttlefish to garden eels. Swim over to the link in bio for

posts.c: [🇫🇷 version FR en commentaire] 💪 I exercised every day in space, pushed myself hard and feel like I came back stronger than ever! But strength is only part of the story. Without gravity constantly pulling on our bodies, our muscles and tendons are used differently, which can lead to changes not only in muscle mass and strength, but also in the way our muscles, tendons and nervous system work together. Sarcolab-3 looks at muscle volume and architecture, strength and power, tendon stiffness, as well as how muscles are activated and controlled by the nervous system, including reflex responses 🦵. Measurements were taken before launch, and the first post-flight measurements took place within days of splashdown, at the @dlr.en Institute of Aerospace Medicine located next to the European Astronaut Centre (EAC) in Cologne, Germany. posts.c: Fall is calling. The leaves are changing, the air is getting crisp, and suddenly everyone thinks they’re an experienced outdoorsperson because they put on a flannel shirt. Before you head out to admire the fall foliage, it’s important to do a little homework. Ugh, homework? It’s not that bad. And will maybe save you on the paperwork later. In fact, a little planning can go a long way toward making your autumn adventure enjoyable (and keeping it from becoming an unexpected survival exercise). 🍂 Know before you go: Check the park’s website for current conditions, trail closures, weather forecasts, and seasonal changes. Fall weather can be unpredictable, just like your uncle’s stories at Thanksgiving. 🥾 Choose your adventure wisely: Pick trails and activities that match your experience and abilities. posts.c: Now THAT’S a power move. ⚡🌎 On Nov. 5, NASA astronaut Anil Menon and Canadian Space Agency astronaut Joshua Kutryk stepped outside the International Space Station for U.S. Spacewalk 101, marking a major milestone in the orbiting laboratory’s power upgrades. During the 6-hour, 59-minute spacewalk, the duo installed and deployed the eighth and final roll-out solar array, completing a five-year effort to enhance the station’s power generation system. With all eight arrays now installed, the upgrades increase the station’s power generation capacity by approximately 30%, helping support critical operations and research aboard the orbiting laboratory. Five years of upgrades. Eight new solar arrays. One powerful milestone for science in orbit.

Home Ice Advantage, Higher Ground, and Striations of Time. As the holidays approach, my thoughts keep returning to Antarctica and how the continent must be stirring to life. With the polar summer fast approaching, Adélie and chinstrap penguins are building their nests and laying eggs. Icebergs sculpted by millennia of densely-packed snowfall glow blue beneath the returning light and provide young penguins refuge from leopard seals. It is one of the most spectacular sights in the world, though I also cannot help thinking of how long it will last between a changing climate and commercial fisheries exploiting its waters. My hope in sharing images like the ones above is that we recognize the beauty of what is at stake and take action to protect it. To inquire about prints and explore more of my work across the poles, visit the link in my bio. From now until Christmas, all fine art purchases come with a copy of my book Reverence.

posts.c: The Catholic Church once put a dead pope on trial. In 897 AD, Pope Stephen VI ordered the corpse of his predecessor, Pope Formosus, to be exhumed, dressed in papal robes, and placed on trial. The bizarre event, known as the Cadaver Synod, ended with Formosus being declared guilty, his papal acts annulled, and his body thrown into the River Tiber. Interestingly, the Christian Church has shaped much of world history, influencing education, art, architecture, and the development of universities. Medieval monasteries preserved countless ancient manuscripts, while churches funded some of history’s most impressive buildings. The Vatican also maintains one of the world’s oldest astronomical observatory traditions, showing that religion and scientific research have sometimes worked surprisingly closely together. posts.c: 18 years of Tiny Desk, 100 issues of NOTION and one cover celebrating the power of music discovery. For our final cover of NOTION 100, we meet the team behind @nprmusic’s much-loved performance series to explore the thinking, taste and teamwork behind a format that has brought artists closer to their audiences. From championing emerging talent to reimagining performances from some of the world’s biggest names, Tiny Desk has spent almost two decades proving that sometimes all you need is a room, a desk and the music itself. Spotlighting emerging talent before wider recognition, and finding new ways to experience established names, Tiny Desk has consistently celebrated the people shaping music culture, often before the rest of the world catches on. posts.c: It's getting colder here in the UK, so we thought it the perfect time to take a look at some bird species that thrive in chillier temperatures! 👀 ❄️ Long-tailed tits live across Europe and Asia. Those living in Hokkaido, Japan, are referred to locally as Shima-Enaga. Winters there are cold and snowy and the birds must nibble on snow and ice for water. They spend their days foraging for insects and spiders and their nights huddled together in small groups for warmth. Despite the bitterly cold temperature of minus 20 degrees Celsius, Diana Rebman (@drebmanphotography) spent hours mesmerised by what she described as the ‘well-choreographed dance’ of a group of long-tailed tits taking turns to peck at an icicle. ❄️ Mateusz Piesiak (@mpwildlife) carefully considered camera angles to produce a series of intimate photographs exploring the behaviour of birds. When he arrived at the sunflower field near his home in western Poland, Mateusz didn't spot the mass of bramblings on the snowy ground -

posts.c: Our new exhibit, "Fragments: Voices of the American Revolution on Lake Champlain" features an incredible artifact: a cast iron cannon that exploded on the Patriot gunboat New York on October 11, 1776. The fragments of this cannon were not only the foundation for archaeological research at the Museum when they were discovered in 1999, they also led to a wonderful 3D printing partnership and innovation just for this exhibit! Thanks to a collaboration with @vtsuarchaeology and the Clinton County Historical Association, we were able to deeply expand our research and display of this cannon with 3D scanning and printing technology. New on the Museum blog, we have a deep dive into this partnership and how 3D printing changed how we can share history. Use the "Read the Museum Blog" link in this bio. Images: 1. VTSU-Castleton alumni Owen Edgcomb poses with a full-scale 3D printed version of the cannon muzzle. 2. A young descendant of Jonas Holden, a Patriot soldier who was injured by the cannon

posts.c: Hubble (along with ground-based telescopes) revealed that the expansion rate of our universe is accelerating! Soon, the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope will study the “dark energy” behind this expansion with its large field of view and infrared vision. Its treasure trove of data will include tens of thousands of exploding stars and hundreds of millions of distant galaxies, tracing the universe’s expansion across nearly all of cosmic history! Hubble's key observations led to dark energy's discovery (even helping earn a Nobel prize in physics!) and the mission will work with Roman to continue investigating this enigma. As we gear up for its first images, we'll share more here on how Roman and Hubble bring different superpowers to astronomy. Check the link in our bio for more! #NASA #Hubble #Roman #astrophysics #space

posts.c: Elijah Wood has some surprisingly unusual stories behind his career. To land the role of Frodo in The Lord of the Rings, he filmed his own audition in the woods, hired a dialect coach, and mailed the VHS tape to director Peter Jackson. He also kept a pair of the oversized prosthetic Hobbit feet used during filming. GameSpot +1 Interestingly, Wood is also a DJ and passionate vinyl record collector. He founded his own record label and co-founded a company specializing in horror films. Despite being famous for playing Frodo, he admitted that he hadn’t actually read The Lord of the Rings before auditioning, although he had read The Hobbit. Like this content? You've likely heard of geysers and hot springs, but what about fumaroles? Fumaroles (or steam vents) are the hottest hydrothermal features in Yellowstone, with temperatures up to 280 F (138 C)! 🔥 Because they are so hot and contain very little water, the water boils away before reaching the surface. Then, steam and other gases emerge from the feature's vent, sometimes making hissing or whistling sounds. Roaring Mountain is a wonderful place to enjoy the sights and sounds of fumaroles, especially on cooler days! 👉 Learn more about fumaroles at: go.nps.gov/YELLhydrothermalfeatures (link in our "Learn More" highlight) Photo (NPS / Ashton Hooker): Roaring Mountain on a chilly winter day.

posts.c: When choosing the images for my book Reverence, I let go of the photojournalist mindset honed over decades of working as a National Geographic photographer and looked instead for the images that sparked some kind of emotion within. The Falkland Islands (Islas Malvinas) are truly a place of extremes, battered by powerful, nutrient-dense currents that pummel the cliffs and feed the towering kelp forests below the surface. The density of life here is staggering, especially on Steeple Jason where conservationists had the foresight to reclaim the island from sheep farming as far back as the 70s. Today the island is under the guardianship of the Wildlife Conservation Society and its natural legacy is preserved as one of the last wild places on Earth.

posts.c: Each autumn, we return to Twilight of the Idols, our seasonal porter brewed with coffee and cinnamon and conditioned on vanilla beans. Its origins precede Hill Farmstead, reaching back to Denmark in 2009. Shaun and Ryan Witter-Merithew first met in 2007. Two years later, as Shaun prepared to leave his brewing position at Nørrebro Bryghus and Fanø Bryghus, he enticed Ryan to move to Denmark to assume the role. They lived and brewed together for a month, beginning a friendship and collaboration that continues today. During that overlap, they established Grassroots Brewing to continue making beer together and maintain their connection to Denmark. Working on their first Christmas beer together (Fanø’s JulePorter), the idea for what would become Twilight of the Idols emerged from this period, taking its name from Friedrich Nietzsche’s text. posts.c: Can you guess the real deal 🥒👀 As it ripens, the squirting cucumber (Ecballium elaterium) builds pressure in its fruits, allowing it to disperse its seeds as far away as possible when touched. It can launch seeds at almost 30mph and send them flying over 12 metres away! This has led to it being classified as an invasive species in many countries. Despite it being a cousin to many kitchen favourites like cucumber, watermelon and pumpkin, the squirting cucumber is inedible due to the toxic chemicals it contains. Can you guess the right audio? posts.c: 💙Blue Interference FTW💙 ✨Devotion/Resistance/Playful/Banter✨ In most areas of my creative practice, whether painting or other mediums, I am drawn to the slippage of memory and the story that various objects shape while in proximity to each other. I paint small and large scale implied still-lifes that dissolve and emerge in quick loose layers of mostly mono, dual, and tri-chromatic acrylic. I often use interference paint as a layering technique to cast a reflective glow on the surface that obscures and reveals selected areas of the canvas. These still-lives are a form of devotion and resistance; they are a ritual cast through the placement of objects to endure the erosion of existence, whether that is the breaking down of identity, gender, or humanity. While each object holds an aura of nostalgia on it’s own; grouped together they form a playful banter in protest against a life as usual. #bluewave #wyliegarcia #painting

What if your fence could grow food instead of just taking up space? A fruit fence turns a simple vertical structure into a productive growing system, and passion fruit is perfect for the job because its climbing tendrils naturally grip onto nearby supports. The science is pretty cool. Passion fruit vines grow rapidly, spreading their leaves across a trellis to capture sunlight for photosynthesis. With enough light, water, and nutrients, the plant converts that energy into vigorous growth and eventually flowers and fruit. Training the vines vertically also helps you use space more efficiently, turning an otherwise unused area into productive growing space. And here’s the best part: a well-established passion fruit vine can produce an impressive harvest while giving you a living privacy screen. Instead of building a fence that only blocks the view, why not grow one that hides the eyesores, adds greenery, and produces delicious fruit? That’s a whole lot more value from the same footprint.

posts.c: Hello again, M30! This new image shows a globular star cluster, which is a roughly spherical grouping of stars held together by gravity. Because of Hubble's long life, it's been able to observe M30 multiple times and track how different populations of stars in globular clusters move. Hubble can discern incredibly specific details in distant objects, allowing for this unprecedented "long-form" astronomy. Discover more at the link in our bio! Image description: A star cluster seen up close, filling the view with thousands of stars. They are clearly divided between blue ones, which are scattered around the outskirts of the image but more towards the center and are the majority in the bright core of the cluster, and yellow stars, which are present in the core but make up most of the cluster outside of that. A few orange stars are closer to us and appear noticeably larger. Image credit: ESA/Hubble & NASA, M. Libralato, G. Piotto, A. Sarajedini #NASA #Hubble #news #stars #space
posts.hd: Hubble image of globular star cluster M30

posts.c: Keanu Reeves once gave away a substantial portion of his earnings from The Matrix sequels to help fund the films’ special effects and costume teams. Although viral claims that he donated $70 million are exaggerated, Reeves is known for his generosity toward film crews. He also reportedly gifted Harley-Davidson motorcycles to members of the stunt team working on The Matrix Reloaded. Interestingly, Reeves was once a talented ice hockey goalkeeper who dreamed of playing professionally. His nickname was “The Wall” because of his goalkeeping abilities. He also played bass guitar in a rock band called Dogstar and famously performed many of his own stunts in the John Wick movies. Despite his Hollywood fame, Reeves has developed a reputation for being remarkably down-to-earth. Like this content? Follow us for more @dadsaysjokes ❤️

posts.c: A commercial airplane can continue flying even if all its engines stop working. Aircraft are designed to glide using their wings, and a typical passenger jet can travel roughly 15 to 20 kilometres horizontally for every kilometre of altitude it loses. In 1983, an Air Canada Boeing 767 famously glided to a safe emergency landing after running out of fuel, earning the nickname “Gimli Glider.” Interestingly, airplane wings can flex several metres without breaking, allowing them to absorb turbulence and withstand enormous forces. Modern passenger jets also fly at altitudes where temperatures can drop below −50°C, yet passengers remain comfortable inside pressurized cabins. Despite their enormous size, commercial aviation remains one of the safest forms of long-distance transportation. Like this content? Follow us for more @dadsaysjokes ❤️

A moment frozen in time 🐦 “‘Bridge of Peace’ was my reward after waiting for hours on my boat. A group of African skimmers began skimming just in front of me, and it was fascinating to watch them and see a few of them even catch a few fish. The sun was just setting at the time, so I got some beautiful light coming in, and eventually I managed to get this photo. I really like its wing placement, as it’s almost as though the bird has become a bridge. African skimmers are very hard to photograph, because they’re migratory birds that only come for certain parts of the year. So, I was really lucky to be able to photograph one.” – Oscar Whitfield This week's #WPY62 guest is Oscar Whitfield. Oscar’s image ‘Labour of Love’ was the Young Grand Title Winner in this year’s competition. posts.c: It’s about time we talked about this… This tall clock was made by Thomas Wagstaffe, a renowned Quaker clockmaker based in London. It’s also one of the oldest objects in the collection at @hamptonnps, originally commissioned in 1760 by Captain Charles Ridgely. That means it’s been keeping track of time for more than 260 years, give or take. You might say it’s been around the clock a few times. Clocks like this are often called grandfather clocks, and this one is an eight-day clock, meaning it can keep ticking for eight days on a single winding. That’s a full week of punctuality, plus a day of grace. Even clocks appreciate a long weekend. Not bad for something made before electricity or smartphones. Of course, there’s a catch. The clock still needs to be wound regularly, or it will eventually run out of time. Video shows a curator wearing gloves as they carefully wind the historic clock. The sound of the winding mechanism and the clock’s chimes can be heard. NPS.
posts.hd: 1760 tall clock by Thomas Wagstaffe at Hampton

posts.c: If you recognize this funky little seed in the first place, you may be wondering why you haven't seen too many of them this fall... Well, we have answers! The results of our annual survey of tree nuts (called "hard mast" by foresters) looking at the crop of beech nuts, pictured here, and acorns state-wide are in: 2026 was a spotty year. Except for a few isolated sites high in the mountains and far to the north, most beech stands in Vermont saw total crop failure. Acorn production was more variable, with some sites yielding bumper crops and others just a stone's throw away yielding very little. Generally speaking, northern Vermont had a rough acorn year while southern and central Vermont faired better. It should be noted that none of this is cause for alarm! Mast production naturally cycles year to year and species to species. Wildlife like deer, turkey, bears and squirrels that depend on beech nuts and acorns in this part of their range have adapted accordingly. What this does mean is

posts.c: Peak cycle! A flashback from my cycle test 5 days after return to Earth from the @iss. A mask collects the air we exhale to measure the amount of CO2 we exhale (our metabolic rate), and electrodes measure our heart rate and rhythm. Our scientists and doctors use these data to ensure all is well with our cardiovascular snd respiratory systems. Just 5 days after landing and I exceeded my performance from my last test before the flight! Yet another indication that our exercise equipment on the ISS not only maintains, but can increase our fitness level even while in microgravity.

posts.c: Thanksgiving is just around the corner, and we’re getting ready to help make the holiday a little brighter for our neighbors throughout the Champlain Valley! Feeding Champlain Valley is looking for donations of turkeys and holiday sides to help make sure everyone has a seat at the table this Thanksgiving. Rob Meehan, Director of Feeding Champlain Valley, has noticed an increase in people seeking food assistance since expanded work requirements for 3SquaresVT (SNAP) took effect. This comes at a time when many households are already feeling the strain of rising costs for housing, groceries, and home heating. “We serve seniors, families with children, individuals with disabilities, people experiencing homelessness or housing insecurity, New American and refugee families, and others facing food insecurity,” Meehan says. “Everyone deserves access to food, and we want to help make the holiday season special for everyone in our community.” Want to lend a hand? posts.c: Small plants need love too! So I try to find a fun way to style them instead of just placing them in a standard terra cotta pot. Here, I took this 4” birkin philodendron and cut the perfect piece of cork to surround its roots. Instead of glue a stainless steel mesh base to the cork, like I typically do, I used a low planter to work as the base of the “pot” to hold in the soil. Obviously it has drainage holes for those that were about to ask 😉 I then dressed up the topsoil with live moss and called it a day. It might be small but it makes a strong statement 💚🌿 #plants #plantstyling #design #beforeandafter #babygirl Low planter from @fayraystudio

posts.c: Have you ever wondered how birds stay warm during winter? Chickadees grow feathers that can keep them up to 100 degrees F warmer than the surrounding air temperature. Waterfowl exhibit counter-current heat exchange in their limbs, which enables them to stand in cold water. Other adaptations include roosting with heads tucked into back feathers to conserve heat and staying active by retrieving food stored during the autumn months. 👉 Want to learn more? Visit the link in our “Learn More” highlight! Photos (NPS / Jim Peaco & Jacob W. Frank): (1) Mountain chickadee (2) Mallards on Alum Creek

posts.c: The ultimate group project: studying worlds beyond our own. As we get closer to the first images from the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope, a long list of science objectives await. One way Roman will team up with Hubble is by the different ways the missions will study exoplanets. An exoplanet is a planet that orbits a star other than our Sun. Roman will likely find hundreds of thousands exoplanets with its remarkable instruments; meanwhile, Hubble’s capabilities allow for analysis of exoplanet atmospheres. This work is part of NASA's search for life elsewhere in the universe. Plus, Roman's coronograph instrument will be able to directly image some larger exoplanets. We'll share more here on how Roman and Hubble bring different superpowers to astronomy in the weeks to come. Check the link in our bio for more on Hubble and Roman! posts.c: We don’t need another reason to love creativity, but research linking arts participation to slower biological aging is a pretty good one. 🎨 A recent University College London study found that more frequent engagement in arts and cultural activities was associated with slower biological aging. Weekly arts participants showed a 4% slower pace of aging than those who rarely participated. Here’s why this matters for play. Art is one way we play. When we paint, dance, make music, experiment with materials, or create something alongside others, we’re engaging in the very things that make play powerful: curiosity, imagination, expression, and exploration. The research gives us another reason to take these experiences seriously. Play isn’t just entertainment or a break from real life. It’s part of how we nurture our creativity, connection, and vitality. Make something. Move something. Try something new. Give yourself the gift ofplay. #PlayIntention #PowerOfPlay #CreativeWellbeing #ArtsAndHealt
posts.cp: We don’t need another reason to love creativity, but research linking arts participation to slower biological aging is a pretty good one

posts.c: One of the densest concentrations of geysers in Yellowstone can be found in the remote Shoshone Geyser Basin, on the west side of Shoshone Lake. We visit the area in the latest Yellowstone Volcano Observatory monthly video update. 🌊 Shoshone Geyser Basin is one of the most spectacular in all of Yellowstone National Park. Located deep in the backcountry along the west side of Shoshone Lake, the area has one of the densest concentrations of geysers, second only to the Upper Geyser Basin (where Old Faithful is located). There are over 100 geysers in this region and 40 or 50 might be active at any given time. A trail takes you right by Minute Man geyser (always at the ready!), so it is quite easy to watch the frequent eruptions there. ⚡During the month of October 2026, the University of Utah Seismograph Stations, which monitors and operates the Yellowstone seismic network, located 66 earthquakes. The largest was a Magnitude 2.0. Throughout 2026, there has been very little change in ground

posts.c: A little throwback to my broke college girl dinner era…. Honestly, I forgot how good these things are. Basically everything you want in a pizza, minus having to make an actual pizza. And yes, they’re still just as good as they were at 1AM in college. Here’s how I made them: - Split English muffins in half, drizzle with EVOO, sprinkle with garlic powder, and bake at 400°F for about 10–12 minutes, until lightly golden. - Add marinara, mozzarella, provolone, (or whatever your favorite cheese is!), dried oregano, and a little garlic salt. - Back into the oven until the cheese is melted and bubbly. - Serve with extra warm marinara for dipping. Please tell me I’m not the only one who lived on these back in the day….

posts.c: In this final video in our explainer series about the new deer hunting regulations this year, our Deer and Moose Project Leader Nick Fortin and Sergeant Dana Joyal from the Vermont Warden Service break down what is needed to legally take a doe in the upcoming rifle season. In order to legally take a doe during rifle season, you must have received an antlerless permit designated for a specific wildlife management unit (WMU). If you do not have a permit, you may not take a doe during the rifle season. If a hunter is unsuccessful during the rifle season, they may use that antlerless permit during the conventional muzzleloader season. Visit our website for more information about taking a doe during rifle season and all the new deer regulation changes.

posts.c: Where's the oxygen? After researchers studied 37 nearby dwarf galaxies, they realized much of the oxygen they expected to see was missing. Oxygen is the main element formed by stars, and also the most abundant element after hydrogen and helium. But by using Hubble, these scientists learned that dwarf galaxies can only hang on to a small fraction of the oxygen made by stars. Energy from the low-mass galaxies’ massive stars, along with galactic winds unleashed by supernova explosions, are apparently more effective at driving out the oxygen than current models predict. Read more at the link in our bio! Image description: Clumpy, irregular, cloud-like dwarf galaxy in a roughly rectangular shape is speckled with small, bright, blue points of light and larger, light pink patches throughout. Dark brown and milky white areas are also smudged throughout the center of the galaxy. posts.c: Día de los Muertos has its roots in an Aztec ritual known as Miccaihuitl, honoring those who have passed. The celebration coincides with the return of monarch butterflies that typically flutter away from our region and make the long flight back to Mexico to spend their winter in a warmer climate. Believed to carry the souls of the departed returning to visit their families, it’s easy to see why these beautiful, winged messengers are held sacred by so many Indigenous communities along their path. 🌼🌼🌼 El Día de los Muertos tiene sus raíces en un antiguo ritual Azteca llamado Miccaihuitl, en honor de los antepasados. Da la casualidad de que coincide con el retorno de las mariposas monarcas que típicamente vuelan de nuestra región al norte y emprenden el largo vuelo de regreso a México donde pasan el invierno en un clima más cálido. Se cree que llevan consigo las almas de los difuntos que vuelven a visitar a sus familias. Es fácil ver por qué estas mensajeras aladas se consideran sagradas

posts.c: I wish they had the slightest idea that how much they mean to us. Just yesterday, one of our cats disappeared out of sight for a few minutes as I’d left her chilling in the backyard. These are indoor cats, so they have absolutely zero clue about life beyond the four walls of our home & the little garden they know so well. And in those few moments, I went through an entire range of emotions. From panic to worry, from imagining all sorts of terrible possibilities to the fear of not knowing where she had gone. Meanwhile, 🐈 walked back in, completely unbothered, after her antics. 🤦🏻‍♀️ Also, as a cat owner, if there’s one thing I could recommend, it would be investing in a self-cleaning litter box. It has genuinely changed our lives, especially in a multi-cat household. Ours is a pretty old model, so it’s too big compared to the much smarter ones available these days. 🤌🏼 - - - #livingroom #bedroom #bluebedroom #cosybedroom #bedroomideas

posts.c: In celebration of Native American Heritage Month, we’re honored to share the powerful words and artistry of Joy Harjo, a citizen of the Muscogee (Creek) Nation and the first Native American to serve as United States Poet Laureate. Last year, we had the privilege of welcoming @joyharjoforreal to Longwood for a two-week residency as the inaugural recipient of our André Harvey Creative Fellowship. Rooted in Muscogee traditions and a lifetime of fearless creativity, she brought a powerful new voice to our landscapes and gifted us with a deeply moving presentation that includes reflections and readings from her award-winning body of work. We’re grateful for the wisdom, artistry, and perspective Harjo brought to Longwood, and delighted to share this special experience with you. 📽️ Watch the full presentation at the 🔗 in our bio. 📸 Carlos Alejandro

posts.c: Christian Robinson is an illustrator, author, animator, and designer based in Oakland, California. He was born in Los Angeles and grew up in a small one-bedroom apartment with his brother, two cousins, aunt and grandmother. Drawing became a way to make space for himself and to create the kind of world he wanted to see. He studied animation at the California Institute of the Arts and would later work with the Sesame Workshop and Pixar Animation Studios before becoming an illustrator of books for children. His books include the #1 New York Times bestseller Last Stop on Market Street, written by Matt de la Peña, which was awarded a Caldecott Honor, a Coretta Scott King Illustrator Honor, and the Newbery Medal, and the #1 New York Times bestseller The Bench, written by Meghan, The Duchess of Sussex. His solo projects include Another, which was named a New York Times Best Illustrated Book of 2019, and the New York Times bestseller You Matter. His latest collaboration with Matt de la Peña, M

posts.c: The stars are just the night sky's mice... The first image is Webb's near-infrared view of the Cat's Head Nebula, a star-forming region. Webb can see through the opaque clouds of dust and gas to see the stars forming within. One of these makes up the cat's glowing "eye" and another, with Webb's characteristic eight-pointed diffraction spikes, its whiskers. The second slide shows Webb's mid-infrared look at the Cat's head, the dust shining brightly. There are structures to the left of the cat visible in the infrared that do not appear in @NASAHubble's visible light view (third slide). The cat's eye is reddish here, glowing from inside the dust. The bright yellow ridge along the cat's "chest" shows gas illuminated and ionized by ultraviolet radiation from nearby massive stars. Happy Halloween! Credits: Image: NASA, ESA, STScI; Image Processing: Joseph DePasquale (STScI) Read more at the link in our bio. Image description in comments.

posts.c: When Halloween is over, look for Dracula in a hibernaculum! A hibernaculum is a place like a cave, den, or burrow, where animals seek shelter for the winter. At least 10 of Yellowstone’s 13 species of bats are winter hibernators. In the greater Yellowstone area, there are few known hibernacula, though researchers have identified some within the park. More surprising is that researchers have documented bat activity in Northern Yellowstone throughout the winter, despite little insect activity, and freezing cold temperatures. #BatWeek

posts.c: This spooky season, we're bringing you a tale of Halloween botany! The story begins with a dedicated search for the extremely rare and globally-vulnerable St. Lawrence grapefern (Sceptridium rugulosum). After weeks of combing potential habitat, one of our botanists was rewarded by finding this plant in a unique location — at the foot of a grave in a sandy cemetery in the Champlain Valley! While the location of this find is seasonally apropos, this is an exciting discovery for a more important reason: since the 90s, this species has been on the decline in Vermont. This find represents the first new population in Vermont in around 30 years, and this cemetery is currently the only known site for this rare grapefern in New England! Cemeteries often contain interesting plants that thrive in the low-competition environments created by consistent mowing as well as easy-to-dig-in sandy substrates. If you take a stroll through a local cemetery in the fall, you might be lucky enough to see the m

posts.c: Here’s looking at you, kid 👀👀👀👀 This Brazilian Whiteknee Tarantula is native to tropical areas of Brazil. Tarantula hair is adapted to help them sense vibrations and other stimuli, and some hairs are even barbed and can be used as a defensive mechanism. Many of us know tarantulas for their eight legs and two body segments, but there are other features that are characteristic of arachnids. If you look at a tarantula’s mouthparts, for instance, you will see chelicerae (jaw-like parts tipped with fangs) and a pair of pedipalps, which help them taste and hold their food. #tarantula #sandiegozoo

posts.c: Comment ‘dad’ on this post for an extra dad joke straight to your DM’s 👇 Cars use several types of filters to protect their engines, improve performance, and keep passengers comfortable. Air filters prevent dust and dirt from entering the engine, oil filters remove contaminants from engine oil, and fuel filters stop impurities from reaching the fuel system. These filters help reduce wear, improve efficiency, and extend the lifespan of important components. Cabin air filters also clean the air entering the passenger compartment, trapping dust, pollen, and other airborne particles. Interestingly, a clogged filter can reduce engine performance, restrict airflow, or cause unpleasant smells inside the car, depending on which filter is affected. Regular filter replacement is one of the simplest ways to keep a vehicle running smoothly.

posts.c: If you ask us, the longline tuna fishery in Hawaii is making waves! 🐟🌺 Solid fishery management can make even the less-selective fishing methods more ocean-friendly. Hawaii is leading the charge by making its longline fishery more environmentally sustainable. This means: ✅ switching from less than 20% human observer coverage to 100% electronic camera monitoring by 2027 to track bycatch and gather data for fishery management decisions. ✅ training fishers to safely handle and release accidentally caught species like sharks, turtles, seabirds, and marine mammals. ✅ gear modifications to reduce seabird interactions. ✅ strategic area closures to protect vulnerable species. and more! The future for longline tuna fishing in Hawaii is bright.☀️ Look for yellow- and green-rated tuna caught in Hawaii for your next sustainable meal. Comment POKE below and we’ll send you the best tuna poke recipe from Chef @banchohajime of @sazanamirestaurant straight to your inbox! #NationalSeafoodMonth #PokeReci

posts.c: What is making this sea of sand march inland? ⌛ This timelapse shows the Lençóis Maranhenses National Park in northeastern Brazil, known for its large sand dunes and seasonal rainwater lagoons. Strong winds from the Atlantic Ocean keep these dunes in constant motion. Over the years, the wind steadily pushes the sand, causing the dunes to migrate inland and change the shape of the landscape. Satellite data helps scientists track how remote landscapes change over time. Captured by the joint @nasa and @usgs Landsat program, these natural-color images show over four decades of this moving environment. Video description: A natural-color Landsat time series of Brazil’s Lençóis Maranhenses National Park spanning from 1984 to 2026. As the video plays, large white sand dunes move steadily inland across the coast. Among the shifting white sand are darker patches of seasonal rainwater lagoons and vegetation. #nasa #earth #science

posts.c: How do you think you’d fare in a bathroom with zero storage? Be honest.⠀ ⠀ We designed and remodeled this bathroom for good friends who are self-proclaimed minimalists. Instead, we used a couple of shelves over the toilet… for friends who can look at a little wicker basket and respect its capacity.⠀ ⠀ There’s something wonderful about designing for people who know exactly how they want to live. They wanted less stuff and a beautiful bathroom. ⠀ ⠀ They got both.⠀ ⠀ Design, Build, Photography @renovationhusbands⠀ Hardware & Sink @rejuvenation⠀ Tile @thet

posts.c: We’re not kitten around! @NASAHubble and @NASAWebb captured a purr-fect view of the Cat’s Head Nebula. This long thin structure, made of dark, dense dust, looks like the head of a cat, its eye a newborn star still shrouded by the dust and gas from which it formed. Hubble and Webb’s contrasting and complementary views give us a fuller picture of the features of this object. In the mid-infrared, as seen by Webb, the dust shines brightly while in the near-infrared, Webb can see through the dust to the stars hidden within. In visible light, Hubble's view shows a dark brown pillar of dust, with a yellow ridge along the right side. This bright rim shows gas illuminated and ionized by ultraviolet radiation from nearby massive stars. On the left are some dust pillars seen in the mid-infrared that are not observed in visible light. It's paw-sible to "fly through" these views with the help of visualizations created by (human) data scientists, which bring Hubble and Webb observations to un-fur-ge

posts.c: Higher waters, warmer waters, bluer waters El Niño is a natural weather pattern that occurs roughly every two to seven years and the one we’re experiencing now is on track to be the strongest on record. While El Niño occurs in the Pacific Ocean, with changes most visible along the equator, its effects can be felt all around the world. NASA satellites like PACE and Sentinel-6 are equipped to measure some of the key features of the phenomenon. Video description: Three data visualizations stacked vertically show sea surface height, sea surface temperature, and ocean color from January 2026 to September 2026. posts.c: Hardneck garlic relies on a process called vernalization, where prolonged exposure to cold temperatures triggers the physiological changes needed for proper bulb development. Without enough chilling, the plant may grow leaves but struggle to form the full, well-developed bulbs you want. Refrigerating hardneck garlic for about two months can help simulate winter, even in a warm climate. That cold exposure influences the plant’s growth signals, helping prepare it for the transition into active growth once temperatures rise. It’s essentially giving the garlic the seasonal cue it needs, without having to live somewhere with an actual winter. Once you plant those chilled cloves, they can resume growth with the cold requirement better satisfied, improving the chances of developing well-formed bulbs. It’s a great example of how understanding a plant’s biology lets you work around your climate instead of being limited by it.

posts.c: Here's something to warm your heart on a chilly fall day! These clips of a Map Turtle hatchling emerging and being released into the Missisquoi Bay were captured by our biologists as they carried out turtle nest excavation last week at Sandy Point in Swanton. Turtle nests are carefully excavated for two main reasons: the first is so that we can document the number of successful nests and hatchlings produced, and the second is to protect live young still in the ground from being eaten by predators. The threatened Eastern Spiny Softshell Turtle is the target species in this work, and three sites are managed for their nesting, with Sandy Point being historically the most important; however, other turtle species use the same beach, including Painted Turtles, Common Snapping Turtles, and Map Turtles, like the one seen here.

posts.c: The original orange and black 🧡🖤 The San Diego Zoo and Safari Park care for two of the six tiger subspecies, Malayan and Sumatran. Sumatran tigers, native to the Indonesian island of Sumatra, are the smallest of the subspecies. Their darker coats help them blend into shadows, and longer fur on their faces may help protect them from dense vegetation. Malayan tigers, native to the forests of the Malay Peninsula, have a slightly lighter coat that complements their surroundings. #sandiegozoo #sdzsafaripark #tiger

posts.c: Hanging peppers might look like an old-school gardening trick, but there’s some cool science behind it. When you hang peppers to dry, moisture gradually evaporates from their skin and inner tissues into the surrounding air. The key is airflow and low humidity, which help carry that moisture away so the peppers can dry more efficiently. As their water content drops, it becomes harder for many spoilage microbes to grow, helping preserve your harvest for longer. Here’s why the way you string them matters, too. Threading through the calyx, the leafy cap at the top of the pepper, helps avoid puncturing the fleshy fruit, where damaged tissue and trapped moisture can encourage rot. Give your peppers a dry, well-ventilated spot, and you’re using evaporation and moisture control to turn a fresh harvest into a longer-lasting supply of homegrown heat.

That means it's time for us humans to say "thank you" to the bats! 🦇 If you're a professional bat biologist with Vermont Fish & Wildlife, every week is Bat Week, of course. But if you're not a bat biologist... what can YOU do for Bat Week? We recommend cleaning out your bat box! With bats leaving their summer roosts, you can tidy up a bat box at this time of year without worrying about disturbing the residents. Don't have a bat box? Well, you are in luck. posts.c: You don’t need a garden bed to grow potatoes, and the science behind it is pretty cool. A seed potato already contains the energy and nutrients needed to kickstart new growth. Once it sprouts, the roots pull water and nutrients from the soil, while the leaves capture sunlight and convert it into energy that fuels the development of new potatoes underground. The tricky part is creating the right environment for those tubers. We’re using @foxfarmsoilandfertilizer Ocean Forest soil to give each potato a consistent growing medium with nutrients to support early growth. Potatoes need consistent moisture, but soil that stays too wet can limit oxygen around the roots and encourage rot. Good drainage helps maintain that balance, which is why the container you choose can make a bigger difference than you might expect. That’s what makes this potato experiment so interesting. Different containers can change how quickly soil dries out, how much heat it holds, and how easily excess water escapes. B

posts.c: This planet is haunted! 👻 The ghosts of volcanic eruptions, asteroid strikes, and evaporated lakes here on Earth are visible in echoes seen from space. Explore some of the places on our planet still haunted by the past. A volcanic eruption about 4,000 years ago created the eerily named Deception Island. The horseshoe-shaped island is actually the exposed part of a volcano itself, while the harbor in its center is a phantom of that massive volcanic eruption. As the volcano’s magma chamber emptied, the sudden drop in pressure inside the volcano caused the top to collapse and form a caldera — now called Port Foster. Image description: Landsat 8 image of Deception Island. It is horseshoe shaped and mostly rocky brown. The thin arch of rock comes to a ridge that runs the length of the island, along its center, like a backbone. posts.c: Ever look at all the rain hitting your roof and wonder how much water you’re letting go to waste? A rainwater capture system puts that water to work. Every inch of rain falling on a 1,000-square-foot roof can produce around 600 gallons of water. Gutters collect the runoff and direct it into a system that can help keep your garden watered. The science is all about collecting and filtering water before it reaches storage. A leaf filter catches larger debris, while a first flush diverter sends the dirtiest initial runoff away from the tank. This matters because dust, bird droppings, and other contaminants can build up on your roof between rainfalls. Removing that initial runoff helps keep your stored water cleaner. This rainwater capture system stores up to 5,750 gallons across the property, with underground pipes directing collected water into a main 5,000-gallon tank. That stored supply can then help irrigate the garden during dry spells, reducing reliance on municipal water. It’s a pra

We asked this 8-year-old to draw the famous “Cosmic Cliffs” hidden within the Carina Nebula, based on the famous James Webb Space Telescope image. The region is actually the edge of a gigantic, gaseous cavity within NGC 3324, roughly 7,600 light-years away. The cavernous area has been carved from the nebula by the intense ultraviolet radiation and stellar winds from extremely massive, hot, young stars located in the center of the bubble, above the area shown in this image. The high-energy radiation from these stars is sculpting the nebula’s wall by slowly eroding it away. Our artist managed to capture the beauty of this Webb image, along with her version of the telescope itself, a rocket ship, and there is even a cameo of "The Traveler" exploring the cosmos! Optical illusions happen because your eyes send information to your brain, and your brain immediately starts making educated guesses about what it is seeing. Usually that works perfectly, but certain patterns, colors, shadows, and shapes can trick those shortcuts, making still images appear to move or identical lines look completely different. The best part is that even after someone explains the illusion, your brain may still refuse to cooperate. You can literally know two squares are the same color and your brain will look you dead in the eye and say, “No, they absolutely are not.” Like this content? Follow us for more @dadsaysjokes ❤️

Tomorrow, Elias Weiss Friedman, a.k.a. @TheDogist, is launching a brand dedicated to pet wellness, @TheDogistCompany, starting with an antioxidant soft-chew supplement. “This was a type of product that didn’t exist,” Friedman tells Forbes Vetted’s managing editor (and resident pet expert) Emmy Favilla of the Vitality antioxidant supplement, noting that it aims to fill a gap in the market and take the place of a multivitamin. Formulated with Dr. Angela Rollins, a board-certified veterinary nutritionist and clinical professor at the University of Tennessee College of Veterinary Medicine (@utcvm), Vitality intends to reduce inflammation and support overall wellness, especially for picky eaters who aren’t eager for fruits and veggies, like Friedman’s own dog, Elsa. 🐶 The chew enters a market filled with pet multivitamins, which aren’t always a necessary addition to a dog’s diet. Vitality will be available for p

Today marks the beginning of a new chapter for The Dogist! 🎉I’m proud to announce the founding of @thedogistcompany and its first product: Vitality – Your dog’s daily dose of antioxidants (available at link in bio). Also featured today on @forbesvetted ! Elsa’s a picky eater (like many dogs), and refused to eat any healthy fruits or vegetables, like blueberries. This inspired me to partner with Dr. Angela Rollins, a Board Certified Veterinary Nutritionist (a rare speciality), to develop a new product that was different from any other dog health supplement on the market. We found that antioxidants, which help reduce oxidative stress on cells throughout the body, were missing from most fortified dog foods and supplements. Vitality was conceived, and after more than a year of development, it’s finally here! You can preorder your tin of Vitality right now at thedogistcompany.com! held.c: Last week was tough for us. We were about to go on our daily walk, Kiki was on the couch while I put her harness on, I quickly went upstairs, and when I came back down, she was laying on the floor acting strange. When she got up, she was panting, drooling, and lifting her paw. It was 4pm on a Sunday, which meant the vets were closed. We had to drive 25 minutes to an emergency vet, they gave her pain meds and told us to keep an eye on her. On Monday morning, she was visibly in pain - as you can see in the first few clips. So we took her to the vet again. They told us - she has no noticeable fractures so you can either wait it out with her pain meds, or do an xray to find out more. We wanted to know more. And thank goodness we did… as it turned out, Kiki had hip dysplasia. One that you can tell it has most likely been there since she was a puppy - some dogs get it genetically. The vast majority of us still do things because It helps to lift up our people, not because It is going to make us a billion dollars. This Election Day I will vote for the hard working Americans who deserve a better and easier path forward, and I will vote against the greedy and power obsessed billionaires who think they can run this country. Rest easy, Captain. We have the helm. ✨ Here is Webb’s look at Westerlund 1, a super star cluster - one of the closest clusters of its kind. Super star clusters are young and contain more than 10,000 times the mass of the Sun packed into a small volume. Westerlund 1 is the most massive yet identified in our galaxy, with 50,000 to 100,000 times the mass of the Sun contained within a region less than six light-years across. Super star clusters are one of the most extreme environments in which stars and planets can form. Because our galaxy is past its peak of star formation, and because such stars live relatively short lives, only a few of these clusters still exist to give us clues to that past era. What if you could turn a chicken into part of the process of growing a giant pumpkin? When Gucci, one of my original hens, passed away, I buried her beneath an Atlantic Giant pumpkin. Here’s the cool part: as bacteria and fungi break down organic matter, they recycle nutrients back into the soil. Plants can’t use all those nutrients immediately, though. Decomposition transforms them into forms roots can absorb, making decomposers an incredibly important part of a healthy garden. But growing a giant pumpkin takes more than nutrient-rich soil. I buried the vines so more nodes could develop roots, giving the plant additional access to water and nutrients. I removed competing flowers and fruits to focus the plant’s resources on one pumpkin, then added sand and plywood underneath to support its growing weight. Even with all those tricks, powdery mildew showed up and eventually slowed its growth. That’s what makes giant vegetables so fascinating: genetics, photosynthesis, growing conditions,

What’s Up is Walworth’s fourth album as Told Slant, the moniker under which, since 2012, they’ve released aching albums of spacious, raw-nerves indie rock. This one is their New York record, a collection of songs about watching your hometown change and feeling the ways it has in turn changed you. It’s a record about commitment to a precarious music life, and all the beauty and indignities that come with it. held.c: 10 years ago today, we received a mention from a man named Brant. What followed was an interaction that has quite literally changed my life. Brant received a lot of criticism for his words that day, but 2016 was a different, more graceful internet, and he rolled with the punches. He wore the “they’re good dogs Brent” merch we sent him, his Simpson’s themed wedding cake featured Santa’s Little Helper holding a sign featuring the phrase, and best of all, 2 years later, Brant got a dog. Completing potentially the most wholesome, full circle meme to ever exist. We haven’t heard from him in a few years, but Brant, wherever you are, give Charlie a hug from us ❤️
